title: From Source Code to Machine Instructions
summary: This unit traces the path from C source code through the compiler and binary file (Binärdatei) to machine instructions and disassembly. It covers the instruction set architecture (ISA; Befehlssatzarchitektur), RISC vs. CISC, RISC-V, instruction formats, instruction classes, registers, and integer arithmetic (ganzzahlige Arithmetik).
keyFacts: The ISA specifies which machine instructions a processor can execute.
The compiler knows the target ISA and operating system and translates source code into a binary program.
A binary file contains program code, initial values, and metadata; its format and contents depend on the operating system and hardware.
The .text section of a binary file contains executable program code.
Disassembly represents encoded machine instructions as readable assembly instructions.
Assembly language is the lowest directly readable level of abstraction. It uses primitive instructions and requires explicit resource management.
RISC uses a reduced, simple base instruction set; CISC uses an extensive instruction set.
The classical RISC/CISC distinction only partly describes modern implementations.
RISC-V is an open, deliberately simple, extensible ISA.
The RISC-V base instruction set focuses on integers; extensions can include floating-point and vector operations, among others.
A machine instruction encodes an operation, or opcode, and its operands.
Instructions can have a uniform fixed length or a variable length.
The three basic instruction classes are arithmetic and logical operations, data transfer, and control flow.
In add a, b, c, b and c are source operands, and a is the destination operand.
Registers are a small number of quickly accessible storage locations in the processor; each stores one word at the ISA's width.
The zero register x0 always contains zero; load and store instructions move data between registers and memory.

questions.prompt: What does ISA stand for, and what does it specify?

options.text: Input Signal Arrangement; it specifies character encoding.
Instruction Set Architecture; it specifies which machine instructions a processor can execute.
Instruction Storage Allocation; it specifies only the size of main memory.
Internal Software Access; it describes only compiler options.

questions.explanation: ISA stands for Instruction Set Architecture. It defines the machine instructions that can be executed and serves as the interface between software and the processor.

questions.prompt: The compiler knows the target ___ and translates the source code into a binary program.

options.text: Metadata
Disassembly
Font
ISA

questions.explanation: The compiler must know the target ISA so that it can generate appropriate machine instructions.

questions.prompt: Select all correct statements about a generated binary file. More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: It contains program code, initial values, and metadata.
It remains readily readable as C source code.
It becomes an executable program only after running objdump -h.
Its format and contents depend on the operating system and hardware.

questions.explanation: A binary file contains initial values and metadata as well as code, and is tailored to the operating system and hardware. After translation, it is not readily readable as C code.

questions.prompt:
Which step belongs between the source code and the binary file?

```mermaid
flowchart LR
 A["C source code"] --> B["?"]
 B --> C["Binary file"]
```

options.text: Register set
Disassembler
Compiler
Zero register

questions.explanation: The compiler translates the C source code into a binary program.

questions.prompt: Which section of a binary file contains executable program code?

options.text: `<main>`
`sp`
`argv`
`.text`

questions.explanation: `.text` is the code section of the binary file. By contrast, `<main>` is the name of a routine.

questions.prompt: During disassembly, encoded machine instructions are represented again as readable assembly instructions.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Disassembly makes encoded machine instructions readable as assembly instructions; it does not simply reconstruct the original C source code.

questions.prompt: Which description fits assembly language?

options.text: A high-level language with complex data structures and automatic resource management.
An operating system interface that does not describe machine instructions.
A representation of header metadata only, with no instructions.
The lowest level of abstraction directly readable by users, using primitive instructions.

questions.explanation: Assembly language describes elementary computational steps and requires explicit management of resources, storage locations, and data transfers.

questions.prompt: Select all correct statements about RISC in the classical comparison. More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: RISC has a reduced, simple base instruction set.
Individual instructions typically perform a particularly large number of complex steps.
The compiler takes on a greater share of the more difficult work.
The implementation can be simpler, more efficient, and faster.

questions.explanation: RISC relies on simple base instructions and efficient implementation, so more of the work falls to the compiler. Complex individual instructions, by contrast, are characteristic of the classical description of CISC.

questions.prompt: The RISC-V base instruction set focuses on integers, that is, on ___.

options.text: Vectors
Integers
Disassembly
Metadata

questions.explanation: The RISC-V base instruction set handles integers. Additional functionality can be added through extensions.

questions.prompt: What does a machine instruction encode in general?

options.text: Only the name of the C program.
The operation, or opcode, and the operands.
Only the operating system's address.
Only the binary file's metadata.

questions.explanation: A machine instruction contains the operation to be performed and its operands, such as the sources and destination of an addition.

questions.prompt: In `add a, b, c`, `a` is the …

options.text: Destination operand
Instruction memory
First source operand
Opcode

questions.explanation: The pattern is `a = b + c`: `b` and `c` are source operands, and `a` receives the result.
The values from $0$ through $9$ are added: $0+1+\dots+9=45$. The value 10 itself is not added because of `i < 10`.

options.text: `Ergebnis ist 45`
`Ergebnis ist 10`
`Ergebnis ist 0`
`Ergebnis ist 55`

questions.explanation: The loop computes $0+1+\dots+9=45$ and prints this value with the specified text.

questions.prompt: What does `objdump -h count` display?

options.text: A new ISA for the program.
An overview of the binary file's headers and sections.
The original C source code.
Only the values of all registers during execution.

questions.explanation: `objdump -h` displays an overview of the binary file's headers and sections, not the source code or runtime values.

questions.prompt: In this schematic disassembly, the instruction addresses are `684`, `688`, `68c`, and `690` in sequence. If the pattern continues, which address comes next?
questions.explanation: The addresses increase by four each time: $684\to688\to68c\to690\to694$. The values should be read as hexadecimal addresses.

questions.prompt:
What value is in `a` after execution?

```asm
# b = 7, c = 5
add a, b, c
```
questions.explanation: The mnemonic `add` performs `a = b + c`. Given $b=7$ and $c=5$, the result is $a=12$.

questions.prompt: Select all correct statements about the classical comparison of CISC and RISC. More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: RISC has a reduced and simple base instruction set.
CISC has an extensive instruction set; individual instructions can do a lot.
Programming for RISC can require more work from people.
RISC fundamentally requires complex microprograms for every instruction.
CISC is classically described as having especially simple decoding.

questions.explanation: CISC offers extensive instructions, whereas RISC uses simple instructions, which can mean more individual work for programmers. In the classical comparison, complex decoding and microprograms are more often associated with CISC.

questions.prompt: RISC-V is ___ and can be supplemented with standardized or non-standardized specialized extensions.

options.text: hardwired only
immutable
extensible
responsible only for C source code

questions.explanation: RISC-V is an extensible ISA. Extensions include, among others, support for floating-point numbers, vectors, multi-user operation, and multicore systems.

questions.prompt: In the schema `OP | F | Q1 | Q2 | Z` for `add a, b, c`, which field represents the source `b`?

options.text: `OP`

questions.explanation: In the given schema, `Q1` denotes the first source `b`, `Q2` the second source `c`, and `Z` the destination `a`.

questions.prompt: `x0` always contains zero. What value does `a` receive in `add a, x0, c`, given that `c=13`?
questions.explanation: The zero register supplies the value $0$. Therefore, the instruction computes $a=0+13=13$.

questions.prompt: Which basic instruction class does `lw` belong to?

options.text: Control flow
Data transfer
Input/output only
Arithmetic and logical operation

questions.explanation: `lw` loads data, moving it between memory and a register. This is a data transfer.

questions.prompt:
Which label is missing from the sequence of steps for implementing `c = c + i`?

```mermaid
flowchart LR
 A["C statement"] --> B["Fetch operands"]
 B --> C["?"]
 C --> D["Store result"]
```

options.text: Disassemble
Add
Extend the instruction set
Display headers

questions.explanation: The elementary steps are: fetch the operands, add them, and store the result.

questions.prompt: Compiler optimizations can substantially change the direct mapping of a high-level code block to an assembly block.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Without aggressive optimization, a code block can often be mapped to an assembly block. However, optimizations can substantially change this mapping.

questions.prompt: Select all correct statements about how RISC and CISC are classified today. More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: RISC and CISC are labels only for compiler optimization levels.
The classical comparison fully describes every modern implementation.
A CISC processor can have a RISC-like core.
RISC extensions can appear CISC-like.

questions.explanation: The classical distinction is only partly valid today: implementations can combine features of both. Therefore, these categories do not fully describe every modern implementation.

questions.prompt: Which statement explains how Intel and AMD can use the same ISA?

options.text: Both manufacturers must build the same processor chip to do so.
Independent implementations cannot execute the same machine instructions.
An ISA describes only the processor's brand.
Their processors can be implemented independently and still execute the same ISA.

questions.explanation: The ISA describes the shared observable interface. The specific implementation of a processor can still be developed independently.

questions.prompt: Why is RISC-V used as the example ISA in this module?

options.text: It is open, deliberately simple, and has less accumulated legacy baggage than many older ISAs.
It processes only 128-bit values and has no variants.
It fundamentally does not allow extensions.
It executes C source code directly without translation.

questions.explanation: RISC-V is introduced as an open, deliberately simple approach without much accumulated legacy baggage. It also comes in different widths and has extensions.

questions.prompt:
Which mapping of the two instruction formats is correct?

```mermaid
flowchart TD
 A["Instruction format"] --> B["Uniform length"]
 A --> C["Variable length"]
```

options.text: Uniform length: typical of CISC; variable length: classical RISC approach.
Uniform length: classical RISC approach; variable length: typical of CISC.
Both formats are associated exclusively with CISC.
Both formats are associated exclusively with RISC.

questions.explanation: A uniform instruction length is described as the classical RISC approach. Variable length is typical of CISC.

questions.prompt: For the addition `add a, b, c`, in this schema: `OP` encodes the operation; `F` contains additional function information if the instruction format requires it; `Q1` and `Q2` denote the two sources, in the order `b` and `c`; and `Z` denotes the destination `a`. Select all correct mappings.

options.text: `Q2` denotes the destination `a`.
`Z` denotes the destination `a`.
`F` is always a memory address in this schema.
`Q1` denotes the source `b`.
`OP` describes the addition operation.

questions.explanation: According to the given schema definition, `Z` is the destination `a`, `OP` encodes the addition, and `Q1` is the source `b`. `Q2` is the source `c`; `F` may contain additional function information and is not a memory address.

questions.prompt: When the total width of a machine instruction increases, every individual field automatically grows in proportion.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Opcode and operand fields are specified separately. Therefore, a greater total width does not require every field to grow in proportion.

questions.prompt: Why can `add`, `sub`, and `neg` be used for numbers with and without a sign?

options.text: Only `add` works for both representations; `sub` and `neg` do not.
For signed numbers, these instructions are always replaced by `cmp`.
The signed representation is based on two's complement, so the same basic instructions can be used.
The instructions operate only on decimal text and ignore the bit representation.

questions.explanation: The signed representation uses two's complement. Therefore, the basic arithmetic does not need a separate instruction for each interpretation.

questions.prompt:
Assume an 8-bit two's complement representation. What value is in `a` after this code?

```asm
# c = 9
sub a, x0, c
```
questions.explanation: `x0` provides $0$, so `sub` computes $0-9=-9$. This value is representable in 8-bit two's complement; `247` would be the unsigned interpretation of the same bit pattern.

questions.prompt: Which instructions belong to the control-flow class?

options.text: Additions and subtractions only
Load and store instructions only
Jumps and subroutine calls
Bitwise operations only

questions.explanation: Control flow includes, in particular, jumps and subroutine calls.

questions.prompt: Select all correct statements about registers. More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: In RISC, arithmetic operations fundamentally access memory locations directly instead of registers.
Registers are a small number of quickly accessible storage locations in the processor.
Load and store instructions move data between registers and memory.
A register stores one word at the ISA's width.
Registers are always larger than main memory.

questions.explanation: Registers are quickly accessible inside the processor and store words at the ISA's width. Separate load and store instructions exchange data with memory.

questions.prompt: A C program is intended to run on two platforms with different ISAs. Select all correct conclusions. More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: The ISA forms an interface between software and the processor.
An independent implementation can use the same ISA as another implementation.
The same C source code must produce a bit-for-bit identical binary file on both platforms.
The compiler must generate machine instructions appropriate for each target ISA.

questions.explanation: The target ISA determines which machine instructions can be executed and serves as the software-processor interface. Different processors can independently implement the same ISA, but this does not mean that every platform uses the same binary file.

questions.prompt: After a `add` operation, an 8-bit register contains the bit pattern `11111111`. Which signed/unsigned interpretation is correct?

options.text: unsigned: 255; signed: −1
unsigned: 255; signed: +1
unsigned: −1; signed: 255
unsigned: 127; signed: −1

questions.explanation: Unsigned, eight 1s correspond to $2^8-1=255$. In 8-bit two's complement, the same pattern represents $-1$.

questions.prompt: What result does an 8-bit addition with `add` produce from `01111111 + 00000001`?

options.text: Bit pattern `01111110`; unsigned 126, signed 126
Bit pattern `00000000`; unsigned 0, signed 0
Bit pattern `10000000`; unsigned 128, signed +128
Bit pattern `10000000`; unsigned 128, signed −128

questions.explanation: The bit addition gives `10000000`. This pattern corresponds to unsigned $128$, but to $-128$ in 8-bit two's complement; the signed addition has therefore overflowed.

questions.prompt: The words `x` are in memory at `-8(sp)` with value `7` and `y` at `-12(sp)` with value `3`. `sp` is the reference point for these addresses. The instructions in a sequence execute from left to right. `lw r, offset(sp)` loads the memory value into register `r`; `sw r, offset(sp)` stores the register value at that address. `add d, s, t` computes `d = s + t`, and `sub d, s, t` computes `d = s - t`. For `add` and `sub`, the operands must be registers. Which sequence sets `x` to `x + y` and leaves `y` unchanged?

options.text: `lw t0, -8(sp); lw t1, -12(sp); sub t2, t0, t1; sw t2, -8(sp)`
`lw t0, -8(sp); lw t1, -12(sp); add t2, t0, t1; sw t2, -12(sp)`
`lw t0, -8(sp); lw t1, -12(sp); add t2, t0, t1; sw t2, -8(sp)`

questions.explanation: The two `lw` instructions load `x = 7` and `y = 3` into registers. `add` computes `10`. Only option b stores this result back at `-8(sp)`, that is, at `x`; `y` at `-12(sp)` remains unchanged.

questions.prompt:
Which statement correctly describes the process?

```mermaid
flowchart LR
 A["C source code"] --> B["Compiler"]
 B --> C["Binary file"]
 C --> D["Machine instructions"]
 C --> E["Disassembly"]
```

options.text: Disassembly always reconstructs the exact original C source code.
`objdump -h` performs the translation of C source code in the diagram.
The processor executes C source code before the compiler runs.
The binary file leads both to machine instructions for execution and to readable assembly through disassembly.

questions.explanation: The compiler generates the binary file. Machine instructions are executed from it, or the encoded instructions are represented as assembly through disassembly.

questions.prompt: Select all correct statements about instruction formats. More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: A greater total width automatically makes every individual field grow in proportion.
With variable length, instructions can have different lengths and different numbers or formats of address fields.
With uniform length, all instructions have the same length.
A fixed format cannot encode operands.

questions.explanation: Fixed length means the same total length for every instruction; variable length allows different lengths and field layouts. Opcode and operand fields are specified independently, so not every field automatically grows in proportion.

questions.prompt: Why is a single C line such as `c = c + i` represented by several assembly instructions?

options.text: Every C line is always translated into exactly four instructions, regardless of its contents.
Assembly language requires explicit elementary steps such as fetching operands, adding, and storing the result.
Assembly cannot express arithmetic operations.
The compiler first replaces the C line with metadata rather than instructions.

questions.explanation: Assembly language uses primitive instructions and requires explicit resource management. Therefore, the more complex C operation is broken down into individual load, arithmetic, and store actions.

questions.prompt: What does the base width of a RISC-V variant describe?

options.text: The number of metadata fields in a binary file.
The number of permitted ISA extensions.
The number of source operands in every machine instruction.
The number of bits in a value or word used for basic operations.

questions.explanation: In RISC-V, the base width is the number of bits in a value or word used for basic operations. Variants with 32, 64, and 128 bits are mentioned.

questions.prompt:
In the following schematic sequence, initially `-20(sp)=8` and `-24(sp)=3`. What value is stored back at `-20(sp)` at the end?

```asm
lw  t0, -20(sp)
lw  t1, -24(sp)
add t2, t0, t1
sw  t2, -20(sp)
```
questions.explanation: `lw` loads $8$ into `t0` and $3$ into `t1`; `add` computes `t2=8+3=11`; `sw` stores $11$ at `-20(sp)`.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes `x0`, `x1` through `x31`, and the PC?

options.text: `x0` contains the current program counter, and `x1` through `x31` are memory sections.
`x0` always contains zero; in addition, there are `x1` through `x31` and special registers such as the PC.
The PC is the only register, while `x0` through `x31` contain machine instructions.
All the names given refer to variable memory areas outside the processor.

questions.explanation: `x0` is the constant zero register. `x1` through `x31` are other registers; the PC is a special register.

questions.prompt: Select all correct statements about RISC-V and its instruction set structure. More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: RISC-V is not extensible because the base instruction set must contain all functionality.
The base instruction set focuses on integers.
Extensions can include floating-point and vector operations, among other things.
The processor executes the encoded machine language of its ISA, not the original C text.
The base instruction set consists exclusively of binary file metadata.

questions.explanation: RISC-V separates an integer base instruction set from possible extensions. After translation, the processor handles the encoded ISA instructions, not the original C source code.

questions.prompt: You compile the same C app for a laptop with an x86 ISA and an embedded board with RISC-V. Why are two binary files typically produced?

options.text: The zero register `x0` contains a different program on each device.
The toolchain generates a binary file suited to each target ISA and platform.
Disassembly automatically converts binary files back into C.
The `.text` section stores different photos for each device.

questions.explanation: The toolchain generates machine instructions and a binary program suited to the target ISA and platform. The same C app may therefore need different binary files for x86 and RISC-V.

questions.prompt: After a crash, you examine a binary file with a disassembler. Which two observations fit?

options.text: Disassembly represents encoded machine instructions as readable assembly instructions.
`.text` contains executable program code.
A header overview never contains code sections.
The hexadecimal column contains the original C source code.

questions.explanation: The `.text` section contains executable code. Disassembly makes encoded machine instructions readable as mnemonics such as `add` or `lw`.

questions.prompt: You are designing a small ISA format with $12$ bits for a value. How many different bit patterns are possible?
questions.explanation: Each bit has two states. Therefore, there are $2^{12}=4096$ different bit patterns.

questions.prompt: While you play, the physics engine calculates new values from positions and combines bit masks. Which instruction class is typically at the core of this?

options.text: Data transfer
Control flow
Arithmetic and logical operations
Binary file metadata

questions.explanation: Additions, subtractions, and bitwise operations are arithmetic and logical operations. They form one of the three basic instruction classes.

questions.prompt: A database app loads records and branches when it finds a matching record. Which two instruction classes directly correspond to these steps?

options.text: Header and metadata management
Control flow
Arithmetic and logical operations
Data transfer

questions.explanation: Loading data is a data transfer; branching is control flow. At the machine level, these steps are implemented with their own instruction classes.

questions.prompt: A register with a width of 64 bits stores exactly one value. How many bytes is this register width?
questions.explanation: A byte contains 8 bits, so $64/8=8$. The register width is therefore 8 bytes.

questions.prompt: Is this correct: When your smartphone encrypts a message, the processor handles the data in many elementary steps; registers hold fast intermediate values, and load/store instructions move data between memory and registers.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Even complex tasks such as encryption are broken down into elementary machine operations. Registers hold operands and intermediate values, while load and store instructions handle data transfer.

questions.prompt: A `.text` section is $192$ bytes in size and contains only fixed $32$-bit instructions. How many instructions fit in it?
questions.explanation: A $32$-bit instruction requires $4$ bytes. Thus, $192/4=48$ fixed instructions fit in the executable `.text` section.

questions.prompt: A spreadsheet calculates `summe = preis + steuer` for each row. In the schematic assembly notation used in this unit, `add a, b, c`. What role does `a` have?

options.text: Mnemonic: `a` describes the addition.
Destination operand: the result is placed in `a`.
First source operand: the value is read from `a`.
Program counter: `a` is the next instruction address.

questions.explanation: In the schematic notation `add a, b, c`, `b` and `c` are the source operands, and `a` is the destination operand. The compiler breaks the spreadsheet operation down into elementary instructions like these.

questions.prompt: Is this correct: In a RISC-V routine, you can use `x0` as a constant $0$; even `add x0, t0, t1` does not change the value of `x0`.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The RISC-V zero register `x0` always supplies the value zero. Writes to `x0` discard their result, so the register's value remains unchanged.
